teach.e: From Middle English techen, from Old English tǣċan (“to show, declare, demonstrate; teach, instruct, train; assign, prescribe, direct; warn; persuade”), from Proto-West Germanic *taikijan, from Proto-Germanic *taikijaną (“to show”), from Proto-Indo-European *deyḱ- (“to show”).

teacher.e: From Middle English techere, equivalent to teach + -er.
teacher.g: A person who teaches, especially one employed in a school; preceptor.

teaching.e: From Middle English techinge, techynge, techende, techand, from Old English tǣċende, from Proto-Germanic *taikijandz, present participle of Proto-Germanic *taikijaną (“to show, point out”), equivalent to teach + -ing.

team.e: From Middle English tem, teem, teme, from Old English tēam (“child-bearing, offspring, brood, set of draught animals”), from Proto-West Germanic *taum, from Proto-Germanic *taumaz (“that which draws or pulls”), from Proto-Germanic *taugijaną, *tugōną, *teuhōną, *teuhaną (“to lead, bring, pull, draw”), from Proto-Indo-European *dewk- (“to pull, lead”).
team.g: A set of draught animals, such as two horses in front of a carriage.

tear.e: From Middle English teren, from Old English teran (“to tear, lacerate”), from Proto-Germanic *teraną (“to tear, tear apart, rip”), from Proto-Indo-European *der- (“to tear, tear apart”). Outside Germanic, cognate to Ancient Greek δέρω (dérō, “to skin”), Albanian ther (“to slay, skin, pierce”).
tear.g: To rend (a solid material) by holding or restraining in two places and pulling apart, whether intentionally or not; to destroy or separate.

tear.e: From Middle English tear, teer, teere, ter, tere, tyar, tyear, tyer, tær (“tear”), from Old English teagor, tēar, tæher, from Proto-West Germanic *tahr, from Proto-Germanic *tahrą (“tear”), from Proto-Indo-European *dáḱru- (“tear”).
tear.g: A drop of clear, salty liquid produced from the eyes by crying or irritation.

teat.e: From Middle English tete, from Old French tete (“teat”) (compare French tette), from Frankish *tittā, *tittō, from Proto-Germanic *tittaz (“teat; nipple; breast”), ultimately of expressive origin. It heavily displaced Old English titt, a cognate of the same origin, which survives as tit, but in more vulgar use.
teat.g: The projection of a mammary gland from which, on female therian mammals, milk is secreted.

tedious.e: English tedi(um) + -ous, from Old French tedieus, from Late Latin taediōsus, from Latin taedium (“weariness, tedium”).

teem.e: From Middle English temen (“to bear, to support”), from Anglian Old English tēman (“to give birth”) (West Saxon Old English tīeman), from Proto-West Germanic *taumijan (“to bridle”), from Proto-Germanic *taumijaną, from *taumaz ("bridle", continued in Modern English as team).
From Middle English temen (“to drain”), from Old Norse tœma, from Proto-Germanic *tōmijaną (“to empty, make empty”).

teeth.e: From Middle English teth, plural of tothe, from Old English tēþ, nominative plural of tōþ, from earlier *tœ̄þ, from Proto-Germanic *tanþiz, nominative plural of *tanþs, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃dóntes, nominative plural of *h₃dónts.
teeth.g: The ability to be enforced, or to be enforced to any useful effect.

teil.e: From Old French teil, til, from Latin tilia.

tell.e: From Middle English tellen (“to count, tell”), from Old English tellan (“to count, tell”), from Proto-West Germanic *talljan, from Proto-Germanic *taljaną, *talzijaną (“to count, enumerate”), from Proto-Germanic *talą, *talō (“number, counting”), from Proto-Indo-European *dol- (“calculation, fraud”).
tell.g: Mental senses related to determining, reckoning, or perceiving

tell.e: From Arabic تَلّ (tall, “hill, elevation”) or Hebrew תֵּל (tél, “hill”), from Proto-Semitic *tall- (“hill”).
tell.g: A hill or mound, originally and especially in the Middle East, over or consisting of the ruins of ancient settlements.

telling.e: Gerund from the verb tell, from tell + -ing.

temper.e: From Middle English temperen, tempren, from Old English ġetemprian, temprian, borrowed from Latin temperō (“(transitive) to divide or proportion duly, to moderate, to regulate; (intransitive) to be moderate, temperate”), from tempus (“time, fit season”).
temper.g: A general tendency or orientation towards a certain type of mood, a volatile state; a habitual way of thinking, behaving or reacting.

temperance.e: Temperantem is the accusative singular form of temperāns (“restrained, self-controlled”), the present participle of temperō (“to moderate, temper; to be moderate or temperate; to govern, manage; etc.”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *temh₁- (“to cut”) or *temp-, *ten- (“to extend, stretch”).
temperance.g: Moderation or self-control in any action; control of the desire to act emotionally; calmness; (countable) an instance of this.

tempered.e: Partly from Middle English temperd, temprede, from Old English temprode, first and third person singular preterit of Old English temprian; and partly from Middle English tempred, i-tempred, from Old English ġetemprod. Equivalent to temper + -ed.

tempest.e: From Old French tempeste (French tempête), from Latin tempestas (“storm”), from tempus (“time, weather”).
tempest.g: A storm, especially one with severe winds.

tempestuous.e: From Late Middle English tempestious, tempestous, tempestuous (“stormy, turbulent, tempestuous”), from Anglo-Norman tempestous, and Old French tempesteus, tempestos, tempestous, tempestuose (modern French tempétueux), and directly from its etymon Latin tempestuōsus (“stormy, turbulent, tempestuous; impetuous”).
tempestuous.g: Of, pertaining to, or resembling, a tempest; also, of a place: frequently experiencing tempests; (very) stormy.

temple.e: From Middle English temple, from Old English templ, tempel, borrowed from Latin templum (“shrine, temple, area for auspices”).
From Middle English temple, from Old French temple, from Vulgar Latin *temp(u)la, from Latin tempora (“the temples”), plural of tempus (“temple, head, face”).
temple.g: The slightly flatter region, on either side of the head of a vertebrate, including a human, behind the eye and forehead, above the zygomatic

temporal.e: From Middle English temporal, temporel (“transitory, worldly, material, of secular society”), from Old French temporel or Latin temporālis (“of time (in grammar), temporary, relating to time as opposed to eternity”), from tempus (“time, period, opportunity”) + -ālis.
temporal.g: Of or relating to the material world, as opposed to sacred or clerical.

temporal.e: From Middle English, from Middle French timporal, temporal, from Late Latin temporālis, from tempora (“the temples of the head”) + -ālis (“-al”, adjectival suffix).
temporal.g: Of or situated in the temples of the head or the sides of the skull behind the orbits.

temporary.e: Borrowed from Latin temporarius, from tempus (“time”).
temporary.g: Not permanent; existing only for a period or periods of time.

tempt.e: From Middle English tempten, from Old French tempter (French: tenter), from Latin temptare, from tentare (“to handle, touch, try, test, tempt”), frequentative of tendere (“to stretch”).
tempt.g: To provoke someone to do wrong, especially by promising a reward; to entice.

temptation.e: From Old French temptacion, from Latin temptatio. Morphologically tempt + -ation.

tempter.e: From Middle English tempter, temptere, temptour, temptoure, from Old French tempter, temptere, tenteor, Anglo-Norman tempteour, temptur and Middle English tempten (“to tempt”); equivalent to tempt + -er.
tempter.g: Someone or something that tempts, especially a man that tempts.

ten.e: From Middle English ten, tene, from Old English tīen, from Proto-West Germanic *tehun, from Proto-Germanic *tehun, from Proto-Indo-European *déḱm̥.
ten.g: The number occurring after nine and before eleven, represented in Arabic numerals (base ten) as 10 and in Roman numerals as X.

tenant.e: From Middle English tenaunt, from Anglo-Norman tenaunt and Old French tenant, present participle of tenir (“to hold”), from Latin tenēre (“hold, keep”).
tenant.g: One who holds a lease (a tenancy).

tenant.e: Possibly just a modification of tenet, but note obsolete tenent (“tenet”).

tend.e: From Middle English tenden, from Middle French tendre, from Old French tendre (“to stretch, stretch out, hold forth, offer, tender”), from Latin tendere (“to stretch, stretch out, extend, spread out”).
tend.g: To make a tender of; to offer or tender.

tend.e: From Middle English tenden (“to pay attention to”), by apheresis of attenden (“to attend”) or entenden (“to intend”).
tend.g: To look after (e.g. an ill person.)

tender.e: From Middle English tender, tendere, from Anglo-Norman tendre, Old French tendre, from Latin tener, tenerum (“soft, delicate”).
tender.g: Sensitive or painful to the touch.

tender.e: From Middle English tendren, from the adjective (see above).
tender.g: To make tender or delicate; to weaken.

tenderness.g: Quality, state or condition of being tender.

tendon.e: Borrowed from French tendon or Medieval Latin tendō, from Ancient Greek τένων (ténōn, “sinew, tendon”), modified by association with the verb tendō (“to stretch”).
tendon.g: A tough band of flexible but inelastic fibrous collagen tissue that connects a muscle with its bony attachment and transmits the force which

tendon.e: Borrowed from Japanese 天丼 (tendon), clipping of 天ぷら丼 (tenpura donburi).
tendon.g: Tempura donburi, a bowl of rice topped with vegetables or seafood fried in batter.

tendril.e: From Middle French tendrillon (“bud, shoot, cartilage”), perhaps a diminutive of tendron (“cartilage”), from Old French tendre (“soft”) (see tender (adjective)), or else from Latin tendere (“to stretch, extend”) (see tender (verb)).
tendril.g: A thin, spirally coiling stem that attaches a plant to its support.

tenon.e: From Middle English tenoun, tenown, tenon, from Anglo-Norman tenoun, from Old French tenon.
tenon.g: A projecting member left by cutting away the wood around it, and made to insert into a mortise, and in this way secure together the parts of

tenor.e: From Middle English tenour, from Anglo-Norman tenour, from Old French tenor (“substance, contents, meaning, sense; tenor part in music”), from Latin tenor (“course, continuance; holder”), from teneō (“to hold”). In music, from the notion of the one who holds the melody, as opposed to the countertenor.
tenor.g: A musical range or section higher than bass and lower than alto.

tent.e: From Middle English tente, borrowed from Old French tente, from Vulgar Latin *tenta (“tent”), from the feminine of Latin tentus, ptp. of tendere (“to stretch, extend”), or contracted from *tendita as an alternate past participle.
tent.g: A pavilion or portable lodge consisting of skins, canvas, or some strong cloth, stretched and sustained by poles, used for sheltering people

tent.e: From Middle English tent (“attention”), aphetic variation of attent (“attention”), from Old French atente (“attention, intention”), from Latin attenta, feminine of attentus, past participle of attendere (“to attend”).

tenth.e: From Middle English tenth, tenthe. Old English had tēoþa (origin of Modern English tithe), but the force of analogy to the cardinal number "ten" caused Middle English speakers to recreate the regular ordinal and re-insert the nasal consonant. Ultimately from Proto-Germanic *tehundô. Equivalent to ten (numeral) + -th (suffix forming ordinals).
tenth.g: The ordinal numeral form of ten; next in order after that which is ninth.

teraphim.e: From ecclesiastical Latin theraphim, from Ancient Greek θεραφίν (theraphín), from Hebrew תְּרָפִים (t'rafím, “household gods”).

terebinth.e: From Middle English therebynte, from Old French terebinthe, from Latin terebinthus, from Ancient Greek τερέβινθος (terébinthos), from Pre-Greek.
terebinth.g: A Mediterranean tree (Pistacia terebinthus and, possibly, Pistacia palaestina)

term.e: From Middle English terme, borrowed from Old French terme, from Latin terminus (“a bound, boundary, limit, end; in Medieval Latin, also a time, period, word, covenant, etc.”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *térmn̥ (“stump, end, boundary”). Old English had termen, from the same source.
term.g: That which limits the extent of anything; limit, extremity, bound, boundary, terminus.
A computer program that emulates a physical terminal.

terrace.e: Borrowed from French terrasse, from Old Occitan terrassa, from Vulgar Latin *terrācea, from terra (“land”).
terrace.g: A flat open area on the topmost floor of a building or apartment

terrestrial.e: From Middle English terrestrialle, from terrestre or Latin terrestris, from terra (“land, earth, ground”), with the suffix -al.

terrible.e: From Middle English terrible, from Old French terrible, from Latin terribilis (“frightful”), from terreō (“to frighten, terrify, alarm; to deter by terror, scare (away)”). By surface analysis, terror + -ible.
terrible.g: Causing terror, alarm or fear; dreadful

terribly.e: From Middle English terribli. By surface analysis, terrible + -ly.
terribly.g: So as to cause terror or awe.

terrify.e: From Middle French terrifier, from Latin terrificare.
terrify.g: To frighten greatly; to fill with terror.

territory.e: From Middle English territorie, from Latin territōrium.
territory.g: A large extent or tract of land; for example a region, country or district.

terror.e: From late Middle English terrour, from Old French terreur f (“terror, fear, dread”), from Latin terror (“fright, fear, terror”), from terrēre (“to frighten, terrify”), from Old Latin tr̥reō, from Proto-Italic *trozeō, from Proto-Indo-European *tre- (“to shake”), *tres- (“to tremble”).

test.e: From Middle English test, teste, from Old French test, teste (“an earthen vessel, especially a pot in which metals were tried”), from Latin testum (“the lid of an earthen vessel, an earthen vessel, an earthen pot”), from *terstus, past participle of the root *tersa (“dry land”).
From Middle English teste, from Old French teste, test and Latin testis (“one who attests, a witness”).

testament.e: From Middle English testament, from Old French testament, from Latin testāmentum (“the publication of a will, a will, testament, in Late Latin one of the divisions of the Bible”), from testor (“to be a witness, testify, attest, make a will”), from testis (“one who attests, a witness”).
testament.g: A solemn, authentic instrument in writing, by which a person declares his or her will as to disposal of his or her inheritance (estate and e

testator.e: From Latin testator (“one who makes a will, in Late Latin also one who bears witness”), from testari (“to bear witness, make a will”).
testator.g: One who makes or has made a legally valid will.

tester.e: From Middle English tester, from Old French testre, from Latin testura.
From Middle English tester, equivalent to test + -er.
tester.g: A person who administers a test.

testicle.e: Borrowed from Latin testiculus, diminutive of testis.
testicle.g: A testis: the male sex and endocrine gland, found in most types of animals, that produces sperm and male sex hormones, including the steroid

testify.e: From Middle English testifien, borrowed from Old French testifier, from Latin testificārī (“to bear witness”), from testis (“a witness”) + facere (“to make”).
testify.g: To make a declaration, or give evidence, under oath.

testimony.e: PIE word tréyes Inherited from Middle English testimonie, from Old French testimonie, from Latin testimōnium (“testimony”).
testimony.g: Statements made by a witness in court.

tether.e: From Middle English tether, teder, from Old English *tēoder and/or Old Norse tjóðr ( > Danish tøjr, Swedish tjuder); both from Proto-Germanic *teudrą (“rope; cord; shaft”), of uncertain origin. Perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *dewtro-, from Proto-Indo-European *dew- (“to tie”), or from Proto-Indo-European *dewk- (“to pull”).
tether.g: A rope, cable etc. that holds something in place whilst allowing some movement.

tetrarch.e: Borrowed from Latin tetrarchēs, from Ancient Greek τετράρχης (tetrárkhēs), from τετρα- (tetra-, “four”) + -άρχης (-árkhēs, “ruler, leader”).
tetrarch.g: A governor or ruler of a quarter of a country, especially of a fourth part of a province in or client state of Ancient Rome.

text.e: From Middle English text, from Old French texte, from Medieval Latin textus, from Latin textus (“style or texture of a work”), perfect passive participle of texō (“to weave”).
text.g: A writing consisting of multiple glyphs, characters, symbols or sentences.
